extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators / IP attorneys / in-house counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on proving and limiting recovery of lost profits damages in U.S. patent litigation, focusing on the Panduit factors and issues when the patentee and seller are distinct or related entities. Explains threshold standing, related-company limits, and the rare 'inexorable flow' exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for the patented product
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a demand for a patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the Panduit factors required to recover lost profits. Courts look for evidence of actual market demand for the patented product (see Mentor Graphics Corp. v. EVE‑USA, Inc., reciting the Panduit factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of acceptable non‑infringing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: An absence of acceptable non‑infringing alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Panduit factor: plaintiff must show that, but for the infringement, customers would not have had acceptable non‑infringing substitutes such that lost sales would have been avoided. Lack of acceptable alternatives helps establish that sales would have been diverted to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee had manufacturing and marketing capacity to exploit demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee had the manufacturing and marketing capacity to exploit demand for the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Panduit factor: the patentee must be capable of meeting the lost sales (manufacturing, distribution, marketing) so that the but‑for sales were realistically within the patentee’s ability to realize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to establish amount of but‑for profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee can establish the amount of profit it should have made but‑for the accused product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Panduit factor: plaintiff must put forth a reliable calculation of lost profits (damages causation and quantification). Courts require evidence tying the alleged lost profits to the infringement rather than speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity claiming lost profits must actually earn the profits
rubrics_metrics.description: An implicit threshold requirement is actually being the entity that earns profits on the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat lost‑profits recovery as belonging to the entity that realized the profits from sales of the practicing product. If the patentee does not itself earn the profits (e.g., a parent asserting a subsidiary’s profits), that undermines recovery. See Edgewell v. Munchkin and Warsaw Orthopedic v. NuVasive: “a patentee may not claim, as its own damages, the lost profits a related company.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Related‑company limitation on recovering another entity’s lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee generally may not claim, as its own damages, the lost profits of a related company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts reject attempts by one corporate affiliate to claim the lost profits of another unless special proof supports aggregation. Edgewell’s attempt to recover EPC’s lost profits was deemed unpersuasive; courts cite precedent that bars claiming related companies’ lost profits absent additional justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inexorable flow doctrine (rare exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Related plaintiffs may collectively recover lost profit damages upon a showing that profits inevitably flow from one entity to the other (the 'inexorable flow' theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow, rare exception where a parent can recover a subsidiary’s lost profits if there is convincing evidence that profits inexorably flow between the entities. The Federal Circuit has not foreclosed the doctrine, but district courts require strong evidence of this direct economic flow; Edgewell failed to show EPC’s profits 'inexorably flow' to Edgewell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation: evidence that the buyer would have purchased from the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence must show that the purchaser (e.g., the related company or retailer) would have purchased from the patentee instead of the defendant but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of the Panduit analysis and in related‑company contexts, courts look for proof that the lost purchases would have gone to the patentee. The Edgewell decision noted the absence of evidence that ‘EPC would have purchased from Edgewell instead of Defendant,’ which undercut the lost profits claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical assessment of profit flow between patent owner and seller
rubrics_metrics.description: Step back and assess the flow of profits between the entity who owns the patent and the entity that actually sells the practicing goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for litigators: determining who realized or would have realized profits is key to lost profits damages. Analyze contractual relationships, distribution chains, internal transfers, and who bears the economic benefit of sales when building or defending a lost profits theory.
